title: Yasodhara
hookLine: the marriage; in the stories she is his equal, and later a nun in her own right
tomorrow: The first sight: an old man
last: THREE PALACES — COMFORT CAN BE A WALL.

lines: IN OLD STORIES, THE PRINCESS IS A PRIZE.
SHE REFUSES TO STAY A TROPHY.
cards: At sixteen, the tellings say, the prince is married to a beautiful young woman of the Sakya clan. Some versions even have a contest of skill.
In a lot of old stories, that's where the princess stops: a prize, handed over at the end like a trophy. She barely speaks. No one tells us what she thought.
Keep reading this one, though, and she refuses to stay a trophy. She has a name, a history of her own, and a path that becomes hers.

teach.b: Her name is Yasodhara. Yasa means glory or fame; dhara, one who bears or holds. She who bears glory.
The first surprise: the oldest texts barely name her.
The monastic rules usually just call her Rahula's mother, after the son she'll soon have. It's the later tellings that bring her forward, and they make her his equal.
The commentaries say she was born on the same day as him.

teach.h: A VOW TO WALK BESIDE HIM.
teach.b: The Jataka stories say the two were together across many past lives, and that long ago, when the future Buddha first vowed to seek awakening, she vowed to walk beside him, life after life. Not a prize he won.
A partner who chose. Her story doesn't end with the marriage, or with his leaving, which is a few days away. Years after he begins teaching, Yasodhara leaves the palace too.

teach.h: A NUN, AND AWAKE, IN HER OWN RIGHT.
teach.b: She joins the order of nuns, and the tradition remembers her as fully awakened, an arahant, in her own right. There are verses said to be hers, looking back on her long journey.
Different Buddhist communities tell her story in different ways, and some modern writers retell the whole life from her side; the old sources leave a lot unsaid.
But the tradition that kept her remembered her as more than a wife left behind. She walked the same path, and reached the same end.

how: Buddhists remember Yasodhara as the Buddha's wife and the mother of Rahula, and in many traditions as a nun and arahant; her story is told in temple art, festivals and verse, and some communities honor her especially as a model of steadfast practice.

o: the prince's wife, later a nun awakened in her own right
the queen of a rival clan who opposed the marriage
a goddess of good fortune said to bless royal weddings

games.q: what's inside the name — tap the pairs.
p: how the old rules often name her

s: Yasodhara is named often in the oldest texts
the old monastic rules usually call her Rahula's mother. the later tellings bring her forward.
tradition says she later became a nun
and an arahant, fully awakened, in her own right.
in the stories she is simply a prize won in a contest
the Jatakas make her a partner who vowed to walk beside him across lifetimes.

games.q: years after the prince has left the palace and become the Buddha, what does Yasodhara do, in the tradition?
o: stays in the palace for the rest of her life.
leaves too, becomes a nun, and awakens.
games.why: she joins the order of nuns, and the tradition remembers her as an arahant, fully awakened in her own right.

practice: Bring to mind someone who walks beside you, not behind or ahead: a partner, a sibling, a friend. Think of one thing they carry that you may not have noticed, and honor it silently.
If you like, send them a little metta: may you be at ease.

wordCard.voice: Yasodhara. She who bears glory: his wife, his companion across lifetimes, and later a nun who awakened in her own right.

orig.note: Pali: yasa (glory, fame) + dharā (bearing): she who bears glory.

carryVoice: Your line: partner, not prize. A name, a vow and a path of her own. Day thirty, done.
